titleStmt.title: To Harriet Shaw Weaver. Saturday, 30 December 1922
titleStmt.author: James Joyce

seriesStmt.p: Machine readable texts of the unpublished correspondence of James Joyce

projectDesc.p: James Joyce's unpublished correspondence, collected, annotated, and made available as a digital edition

div.p: Dear Miss Weaver: Many thanks for your kind Christmas greetings and the little blue and white book by John Donne. One of the songs Sweet, stay awhile was a great favourite of mine when I sang. It is attributed also to John Dowland and to Mr ‘Anon’ but I think the music was Dowland’s. It sounds better on an old piano or spinet. It was written for the lute I believe but I could never manage that instrument. I hope you got my book. You will need a powerful magnifying glass for it. I used to pore over the pages (when not poring over the advertisement columns of Irish newspapers of before the flood) in the days when the Maker of the earth had not yet bereft me of vision.

I think I have arranged for an Italian edition of Ulysses exactly similar to Larbaud’s, to be published by Stock of Rome. Can you therefore ask Mr Rodker to send an unnumbered press copy (marked in three places) to:
and ask him (Mr de Bosis) to send me back my copy which I leant lent him not by post but by some friend who is coming here. I feel lonely without it. His business manager is:
Both seemed enthusiastic (they may be added to group A). Mr de Bosis’s father (his mother is English, I hear) translated Shelley’s Prometheus Unbound .

I am sending on Mr Murry’s article which Mr Pound omitted to forward you and another. Mr Cabell’s book Jurgen
which Mr Sumner sequestrated is now on sale in America and in a ninth edition. Mr Sumner also lost this case. If you don’t want to be troubled by business (that is to say J. J.) when in the country I shall not write about it. I will let you know about the three operations. The first will be 7 January, the second about the middle of the month and so on. So 1923 enters in full armour.

closer.salute: With my renewed thanks for so much kindness to me during my long troublesome expensive useless irritating meaningless interminable monstruous illness and best wishes for the coming year and kindest regards,

div.note: This probably refers to the Medici edition of a selection of Donne's poems that had come out in 1922.
Among JJ’s favourite English songs were those by Renaissance composer and lutenist John Dowland. (Ellmann specifically notes Dowland’s “Weep ye no more, sad fountains”) (JJ 51-52).
“Sweet, stay awhile” was written by John Donne and put to music by Dowland.

JJ sent Weaver a facsimile edition of The Book of Kells, ed. Sir Edward Sullivan, 2nd ed. (London; Paris; New York: “The Studio” Ltd, 1920), which he inscribed “To Harriet Weaver in token of gratitude and with best wishes James Joyce Christmas 1922 Paris”. This copy is now at the University of Tulsa.

On 16 June 1904 – the day on which Ulysses is set – JJ wrote to the London Academy of Music for the address of Arnold Dolmetsch, a musician who had made a psaltery for W. B. Yeats. JJ hoped he would make him a lute, but Dolmetsch offered a harpsichord (JJ 155).

JJ wrote to Weaver on 22 December 1922: “Mr Larbaud told me that he wants to get to work, beginning next February, on what he calls Fragments d’Ulysse – that is the translation of certain parts of Ulysses and their publication in book form here in limited edition” (LI 199). Excerpts from Ulysses would appear in the Milan-based Il Convegno in the 1920s (“Da l’Ulysses di James Joyce,” Il Convegno 7, xi-xii (November-December 1926), 813-28). JJ here refers to Rome-based publisher Alberto Stock Editore.
English writer John Middleton Murry published a review of Ulysses in The Nation and Athenaeum on 22 April 1922.

James Branch Cabell’s Jurgen, A Comedy of Justice was published in 1919 to much controversy. John S. Sumner’s New York Society for the Suppression of Vice (NYSSV) brought a case against Cabell and his publisher for obscenity; after two years, Cabell and his publisher won. Cabell would later thank Sumner and the NYSSV for the publicity.

As per New York endocrinologist Dr Louis Berman’s advice in July 1922 and Dr Borsch’s similar recommendation in October 1922, JJ would undergo complete dental extraction and a subsequent sphincterectomy in early 1923. With Dr Borsch’s consent, JJ ultimately postponed the operation. On 4 April 1923, six or seven of JJ’s decayed teeth were extracted, with the rest of them a few days later. After seventeen tooth extractions, Borsch performed a sphincterectomy in three parts (April 3, 15, and 26) (JJ 536-7; 543; see also letter to Weaver of 13 November 1922).
